topics.title: MATHCOUNTS Handbook Warm-Up 3 Problem 60
topics.text:
Hello Aops I recently saw this problem and attempted to solve it, some of my teammates tried to bring it down by doing sheer computation. I tried to show them a faster but we had no time, I came up with this exponent logic and could someone tell me if there is a faster way.





Problem 60A cubic yard of topsoil is to be spread evenly in the garden at Prove It! Math Academy. The garden measures $10$ feet by $8$ feet. How many inches deep will the topsoil be? Express your answer as a mixed number.

NoteThe problem was worded and punctuated exactly as the original problem.



My Exponent LogicAs the problem needed the answer in inches I used the conversion measures below $\downarrow$

$1$ Foot=$12$ Inches

$1$ Yard=$36$ Inches- I know this is very basic

So the area of the garden is $120\cdot96$ and the volume of the topsoil to be $36^3$ inches. Then I decided to factor the numbers like this $\rightarrow \downarrow$

$\dfrac{36^3}{120\cdot96}=\dfrac{36^3}{2^3\cdot3\cdot5}=\dfrac{(2^2\cdot3^2)^3}{2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot2^5\cdot3}$

Now I combined the denominator exponents to get $\dfrac{(2^2\cdot3^2)^3}{2^8\cdot3^2\cdot5}$, notice how I leave the denominator unsimplified. Now completely simplify it to get $\dfrac{2^6\cdot3^6}{2^8\cdot3^2\cdot5}$ then cancel out the terms $\rightarrow \dfrac{3^4}{2^2\cdot5}=\dfrac{81}{20}=4 \frac{1}{20}$ which gives our answer in mixed numbers as $4 \frac{1}{20}$

topics.title: This Will Take Time
topics.text:
Here's a made up problem for anyone to try:



Richard and Marcus are contestants in a game show. $6$ contestants are known as “chumps”, while the other $2$ are known as "nerds." A chump is randomly selected to start the game and is known as the "chooser." The chooser randomly selects a contestant other than themself and go into a duel. If they pick a chump, the chooser has a $\frac{1}{2}$ chance of winning. If they pick a nerd, they have a $\frac{2}{3}$ chance of losing. Whoever loses is out of the game. If the chooser loses, their dueler is the new chooser, unless their dueler is a nerd. In that case, a randomly selected chump is chosen to be the chooser. Nerds leave the stage right after a battle, regardless of win or loss. The last chump standing is automatically the survivor. Marcus and Richard are chumps. Given that Marcus is the first chooser, what is the probability that Richard is the survivor? Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.



Good luck!  :D

topics.title: Happy pi day!
topics.text:
Hello and happy $\pi$ day!



$\sqrt{-1}2^3 \sum \pi$



... and it was delicious!

If you don't get the joke...$\sqrt{-1}$ means $i$, which sounds the same as "I". $2^3$ is $8$, which sounds the same as "ate". $\sum$ sounds the same as "some" (it is pronounced "sum"). And of course, $\pi$ is for pie.

All together, it is "I ate some pie... and it was delicious!


What's your favorite $\pi$ joke?

topics.title: Target Number Marathon
topics.text:
This is an adaptation of EZmath2006's version of 24. https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h1604992_the_24_game_v2

This is his version:

[quote]Hello!

You all have heard of the 24 game, right?

If not, click here.

Pick four numbers and use regular operations $+, -, \times, \div$ to make 24.





Well now, there's a better version! :trampoline:



Rules:

1. Give some numbers (not necessarily integers) and a target, the number you want to achieve. Again, you can use the four operators, but you can also specify which others to include, like sin, log, etc.

2. Give the solution to the previous problem.[/quote]

Well, here are my rules.

When you give a problem, give any number you want(whole numbers from 1-10,000). Then, give them four numbers so the solver can use the operations of PEMDAS to solve.

For example:

Target: 12

Numbers: 7, 4, 3, 1

When you are finished, post your solution then post a new problem.

topics.title: Faberge Egg Heist
topics.text:
The Faberge Egg Museum has just opened.



It contains 100 valuable eggs, one on each floor of a 100-floor building.



The higher up an egg, the more valuable it is.



You can only steal 1 egg before you are noticed.



You must drop the egg down into your truck; you don't know how strong they are. They could survive a hundred-floor fall, or they might break from a one-floor drop. All the eggs have the same strength.



You have 2 fake eggs worth nothing. They are the same strength of the real eggs. You can drop them from floors to see if they will survive; if a fake egg survives, you can pick it up to use again. If not, you can't.



The question is, what is the least number of drops of fake eggs required to guarantee that you will get the most valuable egg you can safely steal?

topics.title: Proof that 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + .... is not -1/12
topics.text:
I know this subject has been discussed many times before. However, I think I have come up with an idea to resolve the debate.



We know the sum of the first n positive integers is $\frac{(n)(n+1)}{2}$. For the case of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ...., $n = \infty$. So, the sum of all positive integers is $\frac{(\infty)(\infty+1)}{2}$. If the sum of all positive integers is $\frac{-1}{12}$, this means $\frac{(\infty)(\infty+1)}{2} = \frac{-1}{12}$, or $\infty^2 + \infty + \frac{1}{6} = 0$. This implies that $\infty$ is equal to the solutions to this quadratic, or $\frac{-3\pm\sqrt3}{6}$. Clearly, this is absurd. Therefore, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + .... is not -1/12.
